title: AI-powered biowarfare is coming; the Army lays plans to 'fight through' it
content:
AI-powered biowarfare is coming; the Army lays plans to ‘fight through’ it
A new strategy aims to prepare to “deploy, fight, and win decisively in a bio-contested environment” by 2035.
FORT BELVOIR, Va.— AI is “dramatically lowering the barrier” to creating biological weapons, according to the Army’s updated biodefense strategy—even as it gives commanders and troops a better picture of how biological threats, both natural and manmade, will shape future battlefields, service officials say.
The new strategy aims to prepare the Army to “deploy, fight, and win decisively in a bio-contested environment” by 2035, via new training, advanced early warning, and hardened equipment. But its leaders and bio-threat experts are already working to overhaul how the service thinks about and responds to biological threats. AI will be central to this new era of biodefense, whether advising in the disposition of forces or countering enemy attempts to sow confusion and panic about outbreaks, according to officials who spoke to reporters Tuesday.
The era of AI bioweapons
In 2023, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told U.S. lawmakers that AI could “widen the range of actors with the technical capability to conduct a large-scale biological attack,” a scenario he said could come to pass within “two to three years.”
The scenario is drawing nearer. This week, a new paper out of Stanford described how feeding genetic data into high-performance AI models could lead to a new kind of virus that can infect bacteria, showing it’s ability to breakthrough the immunity barriers of other organisms.
This has alarmed RAND molecular biologist Steph Guerra, who wrote, “As AI capabilities advance, viral bioweapons could become much easier to design and produce and could cause even more harm than the weapons used in the past.”
But AI also play a role in defending societies and militaries from such weapons. “We know that everything is changing faster now and so part of the key to the strategy is making sure that we're adaptable,” Alison Tamasi, the chief of the survivability and effects division at the Army’s Nuclear and CWMD Agency, said Tuesday.
Just as detecting a needle in a haystack is harder than making needles, using AI to detect biological threats on the battlefield is more complicated and human-centered task than feeding data into a model. That’s one reason why the updated Army biodefense strategy is so important, the researchers said.
One key element is new, portable genetic-sequencing kits. No bigger than a computer printer, the kits can analyze genetic samples on a laptop computer not connected to the cloud. That might sound like the sort of thing you could encounter in a doctor's office. But a cheek swab that a doctor might take in a relatively clean conditions is very different from samples contaminated with dust, air, fiber, or animal tissue. And getting analysis in the field in a day or so beats waiting weeks for a sample transported back to the States.
The Army hopes the kits, which can classify a sample as a known biothreat or a new one, will help forge strategies when new ones arise.
You can’t stop biology. You can plan for it.
AI isn’t the only factor increasing risks of future biological threats. New viruses occur naturally and spread more quickly today as a function of globalization. But the military’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic “exposed shortfalls in Army biodefense capabilities,” according to the new strategy.
A 2023 study found that COVID-19, which thrust the military into new civilian support roles and imposed new guidelines on forces around the world, undermined team cohesion, military readiness, and of course, mental and physical health.
The new strategy emphasizes better planning for operating during a pandemic, manmade or not. Demonstrating this capability might just deter an adversary from attempting to launch a bioattack as part of a larger campaign, officials said.
“The challenge is going to be how we do this [sample collection, analysis] in the crisis phase, or worse, in the conflict phase,” said Col. Dennis Ruffolo, deputy director for force health protection at the Office of the Surgeon General and Army Medical Command. “That's really what this is going to get after is is is making sure all Army leaders understand that we have to learn ways to fight through the biothreats.”
Here, too, AI will play a key role, said Ruffolo, in helping commanders better understand the biothreats they face, or even will face, in as much detail as possible.
That sort of understanding, enabled not just by new AI models but also humans collecting samples, monitoring environments, and performing analysis, will better prepare the Army for those contingencies. That adaptation means getting more soldiers to understand that bio-threat monitoring is a new priority, ensuring they are capable of biological threat monitoring, and providing them with the equipment and training to do so.
“I have operators below me who do not have doctorates or [are] not microbiologists, I have E-4 specialists who are able to operate that technology with protocols that I have written, and they can do that unsupervised.” said Army microbiologist Amina Zeidan, with the 44th Medical Brigade.
The strategy makes those sorts of efforts a core priority across training, equipping, facilities, policy, and so forth.
“Historically, the Army treated biodefense as a specialized problem,” reads the strategy. “Victory in future conflicts requires an Army that treats biodefense not as a secondary concern, but as a core warfighting imperative. This strategy provides the roadmap.”

report.summary: The U.S. Army's updated biodefense strategy aims to make troops able to deploy, fight, and win in an AI-driven bio-contested environment by 2035.
report.background: AI is rapidly lowering the technical barrier to designing biological weapons. In 2023, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told lawmakers that AI could widen the pool of actors capable of a large-scale biological attack within two to three years. Recent Stanford research showing AI models can design novel viruses that evade existing immunity barriers has reinforced those fears, with RAND molecular biologist Steph Guerra warning that viral bioweapons could become easier to design and more harmful. At the same time, COVID-19 exposed serious shortfalls in Army biodefense: disrupted readiness, undermined unit cohesion, and improvised civilian-support roles. The new strategy, developed by the Army's Nuclear and CWMD Agency and the Office of the Surgeon General, treats biodefense not as a specialized sideline but as a core warfighting imperative, backed by new training, early warning, and hardened equipment.
key_points: AI is 'dramatically lowering the barrier' to creating biological weapons, according to the Army's updated strategy. Officials cite advances in generative models and genetic design tools, echoing Dario Amodei's 2023 congressional warning and new Stanford work on AI-designed viruses that evade immunity barriers.

AI cuts both ways. The Army plans to use it for early warning, force disposition advice, and countering enemy disinformation campaigns designed to sow panic about outbreaks—treating biological threat detection as a harder, more human-centered problem than weapon design.

Portable genetic-sequencing kits, roughly printer-sized and able to run on an offline laptop, are central. They can classify battlefield samples as known or novel biothreats in about a day, versus weeks of shipping contaminated samples back to the United States.

The strategy pushes biological monitoring down the ranks. Non-specialists, including E-4 specialists and operators without microbiology doctorates, are expected to run sequencing technology unsupervised using written protocols.

Deterrence through demonstration. Officials argue that showing the ability to keep fighting during a pandemic or bioattack—natural or manmade—may discourage adversaries from launching biological operations as part of a broader campaign.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the strategy signals a growing defense market for biosecurity, genomics, and threat-detection AI, and intensifies pressure to build safeguards into biological design models before capabilities outpace governance. Developers working on protein design, metagenomic classification, or biosurveillance will find new funding and scrutiny alike, plus likely calls for DNA-synthesis screening and model evaluation standards. For regular users, the practical effects are indirect but real: a sharper debate over open biological AI models, more government investment in pandemic early warning that can spill into public health, and the uncomfortable reality that the same tools making drug and vaccine design faster also lower the cost of designing something dangerous.
report.tools: To follow this space: Nextstrain and Pathogenwatch for open genomic epidemiology and threat tracking; Kraken2 and BLAST for rapid metagenomic classification; ESMFold and AlphaFold for protein-structure work; Oxford Nanopore's MinION as an example of portable field sequencing; and SecureBio's DNA-synthesis screening and biosecurity evaluation frameworks, including the SIGMA and Common Mechanism efforts, for understanding how the field proposes to govern dangerous biological AI capabilities.
